author: Danilo Arao
title: Discord
content:
Para sabihin ng gobyernong pang-gamer lang ang Discord ay napakairesponsable dahil wala itong respeto sa datos.

Hindi pinag-isipan. Walang pakialam.

Nagdesisyon ang gobyernong i-ban ang Discord dahil ginagamit diumano ng masasamang elemento. Wala pang 24 na oras, ibinalik muli ang app na ito dahil sa reklamo ng malawak na mamamayan. Humingi ng paumanhin ang ilang opisyal ng gobyerno. Ang dating na-block, naibalik na.

Tapos na ba ang isyu? Hindi. Sinasalamin kasi nito ang kawalan ng pag-iingat sa pagpapatupad ng mga polisiya. Importante ring isakonteksto ang pagdedesisyon sa limitado o wala talagang konsultasyon sa mga apektado.

Para sa mga hindi pamilyar sa Discord, ginagamit ang app na ito bilang linya ng komunikasyon sa internet. May bentahe ito para sa mga may limitadong koneksiyon dahil mababa lang ang bandwidth na nakokonsumo nito. Kahit na medyo bumabagal lalo na kung marami ang nag-uusap, nakakaya pa namang mababa ang bandwidth lalo na kung naka-off ang lahat ng kamera (at siyempre’y audio at chat lang ang pinapagana).

Akala ng mga nasa kapangyarihan, mga gamer lang ang gumagamit nito. Kung sabagay, mabilis kasi ang audio call sa mga online gamer na naglalaro kaya nakakagawa sila ng estratehiya para matalo ang kalaban. Pero kahit na sikat ito sa gaming community, hindi maikakaila ang pakinabang nito sa mga guro lalo na noong pandemya.

author: Alyssa Mae Clarin
title: Gov’t grants Mary Jane Veloso absolute pardon after 16 years
content:
May Jane Veloso is welcomed by her family at the Correctional Institute for Women in Mandaluyong City, Dec. 18. (Photo by Deo Montesclaros/ Pinoy Weekly)

Veloso’s freedom was not granted voluntarily but was won through years of struggle by her family, lawyers, and supporters.

MANILA — Nearly two years since her return to the Philippines in December 2024, Mary Jane Veloso has been granted an absolute pardon by Ferdinand Marcos Jr., ending more than 16 years of detention stemming from a drug trafficking case in Indonesia.

“Pinirmahan ko na yung pardon niya kahapon,” (I already signed [the pardon] yesterday) Ferdinand Marcos Jr. told reporters during an interview in Eastern Samar.

The development came after Malacañang Press Officer Claire Castro said the president was “seriously considering” granting Veloso an absolute pardon. Veloso had been sentenced to death in Indonesia after authorities accused her of carrying 2.6 kilograms of heroin in 2010.

She was granted last-minute reprieve following international pressure on the Indonesian government.

Veloso’s lawyers from the National Union of Peoples’ Lawyers (NUPL) welcomed the decision, describing it as a “long-awaited act” that brings immeasurable relief to Veloso, her family, and the many supporters who stood by her throughout her years of detention.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Company seeks to evict Sebaring IP residents
content:
By Aurelia Solaba




The homes of the Cuyonon, Kagayanen, and Palaw’an indigenous residents of Barangay Sebaring, Bugsuk Island, Palawan have been at the mercy of changing tides not just from the flow of the seawater but also from the whims of a powerful company. 




Just like their neighbors in 

Sitio Marihangin

, the community is facing displacement because of ecotourism plans in the area. Unlike Sitio Marihangin, however, 

San Miguel Corporation

 has no direct involvement. 




Barangay Sebaring’s opponent is an entirely different enterprise, the Normal Holdings and Development Corporation.




Cycle of relocation




In 2018, the company purchased the mother title of Barangay Sebaring from the Gabinete family. The deal did not include the islanders’ homes but the corporation wants their land anyway.




Alex (not their real name), an ally of the islanders, said that the residents’ part of the barangay exists because 

“umurong yung dagat” 

(the sea receded) and the shoreline expanded. The newly formed beachfront was beyond their original ancestral domain which was the titled property of Honorio Gabinete and Pedro Gabinete. 




As a result, the community relocated to excess land now known as Lots 4625, 4626, and 4628.

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Budget cuts, red-tagging hound LSPU students
content:
Photo Courtesy: NUSP Southern Tagalog & Kabataan Partylist Southern Tagalog

“Student voices should not only be heard. They should also be considered in policy reviews.”

CALAMBA CITY, Laguna — A proposed P180-million budget cut to the Laguna State Polytechnic University (LSPU) has deepened concerns among students over deteriorating facilities, shrinking learning spaces, and a growing climate of fear amid military-led forums linking activism to armed insurgency.

A student who requested anonymity said that the looming reduction in funding could worsen the university’s problems. “There are still unfinished buildings, inadequate classrooms, and safety concerns inside the campus.”

The student pointed to several infrastructure projects that remain incomplete, including facilities intended for the College of International Hospitality and Tourism Management, the College of Criminal Justice Education, and the College of Computer Studies. According to the student, exposed steel bars remain visible in parts of the unfinished structures, posing potential risks to students and staff.

Beyond infrastructure concerns are overcrowded classrooms, inadequate ventilation, and learning spaces cluttered with damaged equipment. “If the current budget is already insufficient to address these problems, a budget cut would make the situation even worse.”

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: New Bukidnon airport displaces Lumad folk
content:
“We were forced to relocate due to the dust from the airport’s construction.”







DON CARLOS, Bukidnon — Many people were delighted by the soon-to-be-operational airport in Bukidnon province. But this caused the displacement of Indigenous peoples (IP).




Around 100 Lumad families belonging to the Kirintëkën-Ilantungën Mënuvu in Purok 11, Barangay Calaocalao, Don Carlos, Bukidnon, were affected. The tribe is a subgroup of the Erumanën në Mënuvu that has settled in Bukidnon and Cotabato provinces.




Bai Natividad Abi-abi, one of the affected Lumad, recalled that they were rushed by those managing the airport’s construction to be relocated by cutting down the trees in the surrounding area. There were housing units in the neighboring Barangay Maraymaray provided for them, but they were unfinished at the time. 




“We were forced to relocate due to the dust from the airport’s construction,” she said in the vernacular. “We feel sorry for our laundry. Instead of the color white, they became the color brown.”







Bai Natividad Abi-abi shares her sentiments to the construction of the Bukidnon airport project during a discussion held at the community of Kirintëkën-Ilantungën Mënuvu in Barangay New Visayas, Don Carlos, Bukidnon, on September 4, 2026. Photo by Michael Tolang.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: Filipinos mark 54th year of Martial Law with resistance to continuing repression, plunder
content:
Representatives of various progressive organizations march from Liwasang Bonifacio to Mendiola to commemorate the 54th year of the declaration of Martial Law on September 21, 2026. Photo by Franck Dick Rosete/Bulatlat

MANILA — Are they already reaping the results of their scheme to rewrite history?

This was the question raised by multi-awarded filmmaker and playwright Bonifacio “Boni” Ilagan during a protest action on Monday, September 21, to commemorate the 54th year of the declaration of Martial Law. He recalled the response of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. during the 2023 World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, where the president said that someone has to enter politics to defend the Marcoses.

Ilagan related the president’s remarks to the recent development of the case of former first lady Imelda Marcos after the Supreme Court (SC) has reversed the convictions in seven graft cases against her—a decision assailed by Martial Law survivors. “This should be remembered on the 54th anniversary of the darkest chapter of our history,” he said in Filipino.

Anti-corruption groups and advocates flocked Liwasang Bonifacio on Monday, recalling the historic peoples’ resistance to the Marcos Sr. dictatorship, as well as denouncing the corruption scandals that happened under the Marcos Jr. admin

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: On The Fringes | Mentally surviving the rotten healthcare system
content:
Flower blooming outside the state mental health facility. Photo by Dominic Gutoman/Bulatlat.

I refer to the force pinning me down to the sofa. For hours, I negotiated with my own body and mind, trying to gather enough courage to leave the house and go to the public mental health facility.

The last time I was here, the queue was so long that it took seven hours to see the doctor. As the body ached in intense abdominal pain, I tried not to cave in. Today, I arrived at past seven in the morning and I was No. 40. I managed to get a seat. That is already a small victory for the expected long day.

Most patients need to be accompanied. I am fortunate that I can still do this on my own.

There is a certain kind of fortitude required to spend an entire day waiting in a public hospital. But this “strength” is a product of a decaying public healthcare, of a system designed to make people used to surviving what should never have been normal. When the system designed to care for us is also pulling us down, this “strength” is dangerous.

In this hospital, only one psychiatrist is assigned for all patients. This explains the hours of long lines of patients every day.

author: Bulatlat Contributors
title: Truth be Told (Again) | To make a dictator (un)necessary
content:
(Illustration by Renan U. Ortiz/Cartoons and Philippine Politics)

On September 23, 1972, the day Martial Law was announced, Ferdinand Marcos was certain — or, at the very least, he was determined to sound like it.

In Proclamation No. 1081, the intelligence had been “carefully evaluated and verified.” The conspiracy was “definitely established.” The enemies had been identified, the danger had been mapped, and the contours of the crisis had been drawn.

In this world the would-be dictator painted, the Philippines was a country riddled with communist infiltration and armed separatist insurgencies, where seemingly innocent organizations allegedly served secret revolutionary ends, recruiting intellectuals and students into subversion and waging “propaganda assaults” against a government besieged on all sides by chaos. Dramatically, by Marcos’s telling, it had all the makings of a paranoid Cold War thriller.

author: Sarah Raymundo
title: Blood Rush | $100 barrel, super El Niño and Pax Silica: Energy hegemony, enclosure, and national liberation
content:
The AI-assisted illustration of the proposed 1,600-hectare industrial hub to be located in New Clark City in Capas, Tarlac. Photo courtesy of the People’s Television Network

The convergence of crude oil surpassing $100 per barrel and the acceleration of El Niño to “super” status—drawn from projections and reports by energy-market analysts, international economic-monitoring bodies, and climate agencies tracking compound global shocks—exposes the deep structural crisis of monopoly capitalism. This dual rupture demonstrates how imperialist war-making, extractive plunder, planetary warming, and the ongoing enclosure of the countryside function not as separate phenomena, but as interconnected expressions of the same underlying logic of capital accumulation.

The rapid climb of crude oil past $100 per barrel cannot be detached from the escalation of U.S.-led imperialist aggression, military blockades, and regional destabilization. Financialized markets and transnational fossil-fuel monopolies exploit war and artificial scarcity to protect superprofits, while the resulting inflation functions as a mechanism of structural extraction from working classes in colonies and semicolonies. author: Aizel Tugalon
title: Duterte appears in ICC case conference
content:
MANILA – On September 15, former president Rodrigo Duterte appeared for the first time at the International Criminal Court (ICC) Trial Chamber during the third status conference for alleged crimes against humanity.

“When I saw Duterte, I felt a sense of relief. Seeing that he was still there in The Hague, unable to leave, gave me some comfort,” Sally Ramos, a Rise Up for Life and for Rights member whose daughter was killed in 2017 by four unidentified men at the height of the anti-drug campaign, said in Filipino.

Duterte wore a black suit and white polo, with his usual hand-on-chin gesture while listening to the proceedings. Presiding Judge Joanna Korner said that he may leave during the case conference but he did not. Seeing him in his usual stature, the victims’ families said that he looked healthy enough to listen and proceed to trial.

“At first, we were surprised when we suddenly saw him. But we’re happy to see him strong and healthy so we can continue to hold him accountable for his crimes against us. Our prayers have been answered,” said Dahlia Cuartero, another member of Rise Up for Life and for Rights, in Filipino. Her son Jesus was killed during a buy-bust operation in March 2019.

author: Franck Dick Rosete
title: BARMM polls plagued by militarization, fraud, violence
content:
A highly militarized environment may create a “climate of fear” that could result in voter disenfranchisement.







MARANTAO, Lanao del Sur — Upon arriving at polling centers for the first-ever Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) Parliamentary Elections on September 14, soldiers were seen guarding the entrances.




They were the ones allowing voters to enter.




Katungod Bangsamoro, an independent local observer accredited by the Commission on Elections (Comelec), recognized the need for the presence of state armed forces but legitimate concerns should be heard as a highly militarized environment may create a “climate of fear” that could result in voter disenfranchisement.




“Given the BARMM’s complex history of militarization, election authorities must assess whether the presence of security forces in and around polling precincts, however well-intentioned, undermines voters’ sense of safety and their genuine freedom of political choice,” the local observer said in its preliminary statement released on September 15.




Two military armored carriers were seen several meters away from an established entrance at Marawi City Pilot Elementary School. According to the Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP), nearly 12,000 soldiers were deployed across the BARMM.

author: Dominic Gutoman
title: Gov’t urged to respect right to protest vs. Pax Silica
content:
Police arresting paralegal Mara Peralta (left) and Agham member Jona Yang. (Photo by Pinoy Weekly)

MANILA – The people have the right to protest.

Progressive groups asserted this after authorities arrested five paralegals who responded during the September 10 protest at the Grand Hyatt Manila, where the Luzon Economic Corridor forum was held, attended by 600 foreign investors, industry leaders, and government officials.

The arrested paralegals were released on bail on September 12.

In particular, human rights group Karapatan criticized Presidential Spokesperson Claire Castro’s statement that those who oppose Pax Silica should course their objections through “proper channels,” claiming that “proper protest uses reason and intelligence.”

Philippine National Police Chief General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr., meanwhile, said that the right to protest must remain “within the bounds of the law” and urged cause-oriented groups to raise their concerns through “lawful means.”

Karapatan maintained that the arrests were unlawful and arbitrary and impeded the peoples’ right to protest.

“It is the State that carries out unlawful and arbitrary arrests through Marcosian laws such as Batas Pambansa 880. Whose interests are you protecting, that of the people or that of big business who will benefit from the Pax Silica?” Karapatan Secretary-General Cristina Palabay said in a statement.

author: Shan Kenshin Ecaldre
title: Student leader urges CHR to probe red-tagging, house visits
content:
Photo by Shan Kenshin Ecaldre/Bulatlat

Members of the volunteer group were photographed and recorded during the activity without their consent.

MANILA — A student leader and youth activist from Southern Luzon asked the Commission on Human Rights (CHR) to intervene as he and his family were subjected to intimidation following his participation in a humanitarian relief operation in Camarines Norte.

Michael Orajay Esperanza, a student of Southern Luzon State University (SLSU) and youth organizer, filed a sworn statement before the CHR explaining a pattern of red-tagging, surveillance, and questioning directed at him and his family weeks after he joined relief missions for communities affected by severe weather disturbances.

Esperanza said that the incidents began after he volunteered with The Good Samaritan (TGS), a faith-based humanitarian group that conducted relief operations in Quezon and Camarines Norte in August.

An English education student and campus journalist of The Footprints, official student publication of SLSU’s College of Teacher Education, Esperanza also participates in student and community campaigns. He is lead convenor of Rise for Education–SLSU and previously acted as spokesperson of Kabataan Partylist–Quezon.
